entries.text: Building a character in the 56th Century is a guided sequence, not a math test. Steps 1-4 are handled for you on the Character tab - it applies every racial, background, and occupation modifier automatically. Use this section to understand WHAT each choice means and HOW to make one you will enjoy playing, then let the sheet do the bookkeeping.

entries.key: START WITH A CONCEPT, NOT A STAT LINE
entries.text: Before you touch a single number, picture the person. Who are they when the shooting stops? What do they want, what do they refuse to do, and what got them where they are now? A one-sentence pitch - 'an exiled Hakari clan-scout selling her tracking to the highest bidder' - will steer every mechanical choice that follows and keep them coherent. The rules reward a clear idea far more than an optimal spreadsheet.

Your race is the biological (or post-biological) foundation everything else is built on. It sets your attribute baselines and the min/avg/max each attribute can reach, and it grants a small package of innate Racial, Evolution, and Environment traits. Read the lore on the Races tab, not just the numbers - a race tells you where your character is from, how the galaxy treats them, and the cultural weight they carry into every room. Choose the people you want to belong to first; the stat spread is the consequence of that choice, not the reason for it.

Decide how your character entered the world. Were they decanted from a cloning vat - a manufactured life with a backup somewhere - or did they arrive the old-fashioned way for their species: hatching, live birth, mitosis, budding? This is mainly a roleplay and setting choice, but it has teeth: clones can be re-grown (which resets EVO afflictions and matters for talents like Adapted Cloning), and a vat-born outlook on death is very different from one shaped by a single, irreplaceable life.

Your background is where you come from and what your formative years made of you. It grants a set of skills, sometimes an attribute tweak or a talent, and roots you in the setting. All general backgrounds are open to everyone; some are race-exclusive and reward leaning into your origin. Pick the history that explains your concept - the skills are the proof of a life lived, not a shopping list.

Your occupation is what you did for a living before the campaign opened - your trade, your hustle, your posting. It layers a focused skill package on top of your background. You can reinforce your background for a tight specialist, or contrast it for someone with range: the temple-raised Patriark who became a debt-collector is a more interesting sheet than one who only ever did the obvious thing.

The Character tab now combines race, background, and occupation and writes the totals to your sheet automatically. If you need to hand-tune something, open the manual override section via the checkbox on the CS-Main sheet - but in normal play you should rarely need it.

New characters get 50 XP to spend across SKILLS, ATTRIBUTES, and DEFENSES. No skill may start above level 5. The character creator built into this compendium can track the spend for you. See Character Advancement for the full cost model and spending tips. Remember the core truth of this system: there are no levels. These 50 XP ARE your starting power, and every XP you earn for the rest of the character's life works exactly the same way - so spend them as the opening statement of who this person is.

Your occupation sets your starting contacts and your starting credits - the people who owe you, fear you, or answer your calls, and the money in your account - though the GM can adjust either to fit the campaign. Spend your credits on gear that fits the concept, or bank some for the inevitable bad night. A character is the sum of who they know and what they carry as much as what they can roll.

entries.key: FOR THE GM - RUN A SESSION ZERO AND SAY YES TO CONCEPTS
entries.text: Character creation is the first scene of the campaign, so play it that way. Sit the table down together, let people pitch concepts out loud, and look for the hooks and frictions between them before anyone finalises a number. Your default to a plausible race/background/occupation combination should be 'yes, and here's how that shows up in the world.' Steer away from the rules only when a choice would wreck the tone or the party's ability to function - and when you do, offer a reflavoured version that keeps the player's idea intact.

The 56th Century has no levels. A character never 'levels up,' and there is no class track pulling them along a fixed path. Instead, every point of experience you earn is a unit of progression that you invest directly into the three things that define what your character can do: SKILLS, ATTRIBUTES, and DEFENSES. Your sheet is nothing more, and nothing less, than the sum of those investments. Two characters with an identical XP total can be wildly different people depending on where they chose to put it.

entries.key: EVERY XP IS A CHOICE ABOUT WHO YOU'RE BECOMING
entries.text: Because nothing forces your growth down a template, each XP is a small declaration of identity. Spend toward the fiction, not just the math: the hired gun who keeps quietly sinking points into Medicine is becoming the person who can't stand to watch anyone bleed out; the face who maxes Intimidation before Persuasion is telling you how they'd rather win. Let your spend tell a story, and your character will deepen every time they earn a point - something a level-up table can never give you.

XP buys three categories of advancement. SKILLS are what you are trained to attempt. ATTRIBUTES (PHYSICAL, MENTAL, SOCIAL, ACUITY) are your raw potential - they let you reroll the dice on every skill in their category, so they quietly amplify everything you already do. DEFENSES (ENDURANCE, SPEED, WITS, WILLPOWER) are your staying power, your speed and initiative, your reactions, and your resolve under pressure.

Skills cost 1 XP per level, and the cost is cumulative - you must buy every level on the way up. The running totals from 1 to 10 are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55 XP. New characters cannot raise any skill above level 5.
examples: A level-2 skill bought from scratch costs 1 + 2 = 3 XP total.
Raising a skill from 3 to 6 costs 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 XP.

entries.text: Attributes and defenses cost 5 XP times the level, also cumulative. Because primary attributes can sit at 0 or in the negatives, the minimum cost to gain a single point is always 5 XP. Climbing into positive territory gets expensive quickly.
examples: Going from +0 to +3 in an attribute costs 5 + 10 + 15 = 30 XP.
Buying out of the negatives is flat: each point from -2 up to 0 costs 5 XP.

entries.text: Early skill levels are cheap, so a few XP spread wide makes a flexible generalist who always has something to contribute. Attributes are force-multipliers - a single point rerolls the dice on ten skills - but they are pricey and best bought once you know which category is your spine. A common, healthy pattern is to anchor one or two key attributes, then let cheap skill levels fan out from there. There is no wrong answer, only the character you are trying to build.

entries.key: FOR THE GM - AWARD XP FOR THE STORY, AND PACE IT
entries.text: XP is the only progression lever in this game, so you control the entire feel of advancement with it. Reward engagement, clever play, real risks taken, and roleplay that moves the table - not just bodies on the floor. Steady, modest drips (a handful of points per session) keep growth meaningful without inflation; large lump sums make every choice feel weightless. When you hand out XP, name what earned it: that turns the reward into reinforcement and tells the table what this campaign values.

Training is an OPTIONAL framework that the GM switches on or off for the campaign. It governs how EXISTING characters turn earned XP into higher skills between sessions - whether that is a free, abstract process or something that costs time and money in the fiction. Decide as a table which mode you want before play begins; both are fully supported.

entries.key: OPTION A - FREE ADVANCEMENT (simplest; good default)
entries.text: Between games, players simply spend their earned XP on skills with no extra time or credit cost. Downtime and practice are assumed to happen off-screen. Choose this when you want momentum, minimal bookkeeping, and a campaign where the story - not a training ledger - sets the pace of growth.

entries.key: OPTION B - TRAINING FRAMEWORK (grittier, downtime-driven play)
entries.text: If the GM wants advancement to cost something tangible, characters must seek out training to raise a skill. You can buy a course, be taught by someone who already has a higher rank in that skill, or - with GM approval - earn the increase through demonstrated use in play when you've clearly put the skill through its paces. Whichever route you take, you still spend the XP; training gates WHEN the increase lands, not whether you paid for it.

Under Option B, training costs 10,000 cr and one full day per skill level, and every level is purchased separately. If you don't have the downtime to spare, you can still train while busy - but the process takes three times as long.
examples: Raising a skill from 3 to 6 costs 15 XP and 150,000 cr, and takes 15 days of training - or 45 days if you never take time off.

entries.key: TALENTS - YOUR SIGNATURE TRICKS (See the Talent tab)
entries.text: Where a skill says what you can attempt, a talent says what makes you exceptional at it. A talent is a permanent, named capability - a piece of hard training, a knack, a quirk of biology or wiring - that bends a rule in your favour. They are why two characters with identical skills still play completely differently, and they are where a lot of a character's flavour and identity actually live.

You don't spend XP on talents directly. Instead, every XP you invest in a CATEGORY - PHYSICAL, MENTAL, SOCIAL, or ACUITY - grants you 1 TALENT point in that same category. Talents are the natural by-product of growing the skills and attributes beneath a category: invest in being physically formidable and the physical talents open up to you.
examples: Four PHYSICAL skills at level 5 = 20 XP invested in PHYSICAL = 20 PHYSICAL talent points to spend.

entries.text: Each talent has a cost. Buying it lowers that category's available talent points by the cost, and a category's pool can never drop below 0 - so you can only hold the talents your investment genuinely supports. Points are tracked per category and don't cross over: physical points can never buy a mental talent. This keeps a character's special tricks anchored to where they've actually put their effort.

entries.key: CHOOSE TALENTS THAT EXPRESS THE CHARACTER
entries.text: Browse the Talent tab for identity, not just raw power. A talent is one of the best places to anchor a reputation - the medic everyone trusts in a crisis, the operator who simply does not flinch. Look for talents that reward the way you already want to play rather than ones that demand you play differently; a talent you'll trigger every session is worth far more than a stronger one you'll forget you own. Read the effect text and ask 'when does this come up, and does that sound like me?'

Talents are a clean lever for the spotlight - build scenes that let a character's signature trick matter, and the player who chose it feels seen. Be generous about letting players reflavour a talent's presentation to fit their concept as long as the mechanics are untouched. Keep an eye out only for talents that, stacked with the right gear or build, trivialise a whole pillar of play; when that happens, talk to the player and adjust rather than letting one trick quietly delete the challenge for everyone.

Evolution is an OPTIONAL system - no character is ever forced to spend resources in it. It is the framework for players who want to modify their body, install cybernetics, or dabble in magic, progressing a character by investing resources into one or more of three paths: GENETICS, CYBERNETICS, or MAGIC. The full rules - overflow, afflictions, and the per-path effects - follow below.

There is no hard limit on how many EVOs a character can have. Each EVO tier you own adds its rank to your total EVO score. Your SAFE softcap is your ENDURANCE + WILLPOWER: as long as your EVO score stays at or below that sum, your body integrates the modifications cleanly. You CAN push past the cap, but every point over it is a mounting risk that an installation goes wrong and saddles you with an EVO affliction.

Each category has 3 tiers, and you must own the lower tier before buying the next one in that category. Because the ranks stack onto your EVO score, a Tier 3 trait - which requires Tiers 1 and 2 - adds 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 points to your total.
examples: Alpha Specimen Tier II requires Alpha Specimen Tier I, for a combined 3 EVO points (1 + 2).

entries.text: Tier 1 evolutions grant a benefit but usually have a small impact on actual play. Tier 2 evolutions are substantial, delivering significant changes to how a character functions. Tier 3 evolutions provide major benefits, but come with a significant cost in both credits and EVO points - they represent real commitment to a path.

entries.key: EVOLUTIONS DON'T COME WITH DRAWBACKS - BUT ADVANCING CHANGES YOU
entries.text: An evolution does not inherently saddle you with a penalty; the benefit is the benefit. What happens instead is that climbing the tiers of a category marks you, because committing to a path changes your body and your presence. Genetics reshapes your appearance and alters how drugs and medicine affect you. Cybernetics leaves visible implants, makes you read as a MACHINE at the top tier, and risks CYBER SHOCK whenever you fire an active augment. Magic fuses spirit into your flesh and, fully realised, makes you register as a SPIRIT that leaks CHI into every scene you enter. These are consequences of the path you chose, not taxes bolted onto a single trait - the Evolution tab lists the specifics tier by tier.

Installing an EVO is a skill check: Medical for Genetics, Technology for Cybernetics, Binding for Magic, at DC 2 / 4 / 6 by tier. A strong result matters twice over - if the install would push you past your EVO capacity, that same skill result is what resists the overflow check below.

Every character has an EVO capacity equal to ENDURANCE + WILLPOWER. As long as your total EVO points stay at or under that number, your body carries the modifications cleanly - no rolls, no risk. Raising your ENDURANCE or WILLPOWER raises your capacity too, so a tougher or more strong-willed character can safely hold more.

There is no hard limit - you can keep installing EVOs well past your capacity - but the moment a new EVO would push your total EVO points above the soft cap, that installation becomes a gamble. EVOs you add while still under the cap never trigger this; only the one that tips you over (and any installed while already over) does.

When the EVO being installed would leave you over capacity, the GM secretly rolls a D10 while the installer makes their install check (Medical / Technology / Binding). Compare the installer's skill result against the GM's hidden roll. If the installer's result is equal to or higher than the GM's D10, the EVO seats cleanly and nothing goes wrong. If the installer falls short, the body rejects part of the change and an affliction takes root.

On a failed overflow check, find the row on the EVO Affliction Table by adding two numbers: how many EVO points you are OVER your soft cap (counting the new EVO), plus how far the installer fell short (the GM's D10 minus the installer's skill result). The higher the total, the nastier the result - so being deep over your cap AND botching the install is what lands you at the bottom of the table.
examples: Tom has WILLPOWER 3 + ENDURANCE 3 = 6 EVO capacity. He already holds a full Tier 1-2-3 EVO (1+2+3 = 6 points) and a Tier 1-2 EVO (1+2 = 3 points) = 9 points total, so he is already 3 over his cap. He now installs Tier 3 of that second EVO (+3 points), reaching 12 points - 6 over the cap. The GM secretly rolls 8; the installer's skill result is 5. Since 5 is under 8, it's an affliction: 6 (points over cap) + 3 (the 8 minus 5 shortfall) = 9 -> row 9, Traumatic Activation. From now on, whenever Tom uses that new EVO he gains a trauma.

entries.text: An affliction does not manifest the moment it is installed - you won't know how bad it is until it is too late. It lurks dormant until something sets it off.

An installed affliction goes off when you roll a CRITICAL FAILURE during a SCENE on any roll that could have been influenced by the EVO - for instance, a crit-fail while casting with an EVO that grants CHI. An affliction fires at most once per SCENE: once one triggers, no other can trigger until the next scene.

EVO afflictions are cumulative - a heavily-modified character can be carrying several at once. When more than one could fire from the same critical failure, the GM rolls randomly to decide which one does.

Getting cloned wipes the slate: it resets all of a character's EVOs and every affliction they have picked up. The exception is Permanent EVOs, which (along with anything riding on them) stay with a character forever.

entries.key: NO EVO ESCAPES ITS OWN AFFLICTION
entries.text: An EVO can never negate the drawback of an affliction. If one of your EVOs would normally make you immune to an affliction's effect, you ignore that EVO for as long as the affliction is active.

entries.text: Tier 1 — Your new genetic code has had some cosmetic changes on your appearance; pick one or more features (color, shape, hair, horns etc.) and mutate them.
Tier 2 — Lifebane critical effect will disable one of your GENETIC EVOs (player's choice, all 3 tiers) until a recovery roll is made.
Tier 3 — Extensive modifications can impact drugs and medical treatment. Any drug/medical item used on you has a 50% chance of no TOXICITY or double TOXICITY. Custom drugs can avoid this.
Tier 1 — Replacing body parts with machinery leaves traces. You now have visible implants on your body — pick one or more appearance features representing your Cybernetic EVO.
Tier 2 — EMP critical effect will disable one of your CYBERNETIC EVOs (player's choice, all 3 tiers) until a recovery roll is made.

Tier 3 — You count as a MACHINE and no longer count as a LIVING BEING. On SEVERE TRAUMA there is a 50% chance it strikes one of your Cybernetic EVOs instead, negating the TRAUMA but disabling that EVO until repaired.
Passive EVOs: Always on, generate no CYBER SHOCK.

Active EVOs: Free action to gain benefits. Roll TECHNOLOGY vs current MORALE to avoid CYBER SHOCK. On failure the augment works but you lose 1 MORALE per TIER. If MORALE drops to 0 you lose control of your character.
Tier 1 — EVO magic is done via spirit fusion as tattoos or grafting relics into your flesh. Pick the design and modify one or more of your character's features.
Tier 2 — Spiritbane critical effect will disable one of your MAGIC EVOs (player's choice, all 3 tiers) until a recovery roll is made.

Tier 3 — You no longer count as a LIVING being while your SPIRIT is active; you count as a SPIRIT instead. You leak CHI in your environment — every SCENE you start in has at least 1 RAW CHI in the area.
SKILLS

Skills work on a D10 dice pool: roll a number of D10s equal to your skill rank, count successes (5+) against the DC. Your matching category attribute (PHYSICAL/MENTAL/SOCIAL/ACUITY) lets you reroll failures (positive) or successes (negative).
Many obstacles can be solved by more than one skill. The GM sets the skill by what the player wants the OUTCOME to be, not by the obstacle alone. Always allow any plausible skill at a fair DC.

Want it quiet and the lock is electronic on a network? HACKING. Want to short-circuit the card reader? TECHNOLOGY. A mundane mechanical lock? LARCENY. Don't care about the door, just the wall? HEAVY WEAPONS (make a hole). Want a controlled, predictable breach? ENGINEERING. All valid, chosen by the outcome the player wants.

The locked door above is a deliberately easy example: one obstacle, five honest skills. Treat it as a template for everything else. There is almost never a single 'correct' skill for a situation — there is only the destination (get past the door, learn the secret, survive the room) and the many roads a party of different specialists might take to reach it. A talker charms the guard into opening it; a soldier blows the lock off; a scientist dissolves the hinges with a reagent; a medic fakes a contamination scare so someone seals it from the inside. None of these is wrong. What matters is whether the approach makes sense in the fiction and is fun at the table.

Newer players sometimes freeze, waiting for a scene that exactly matches a skill they own and treating everything else as someone else's job. Don't. Look at what your character is genuinely good at and ask: 'how would I solve this, with what I bring?' The wrong tool used cleverly is usually more memorable than the obvious one. You are encouraged to experiment, improvise, and pitch ideas the rules never anticipated — combining skills, repurposing gear, using a strength sideways. That is the game working as intended, not a loophole to be argued down.

entries.key: FOR THE GM — REWARD THINKING OUTSIDE THE BOX
entries.text: Your default answer should be 'yes, roll for it' far more often than 'no.' When a player proposes a plausible use of a skill, set a fair DC (trivial 3 / standard 5 / hard 7) and let them try, even when it isn't the approach you had in mind. Reward creative, in-character thinking: a clever angle can lower the DC, grant a bonus, or simply succeed outright. Never gate progress behind one specific skill — if a roll fails, it should redirect, cost something, or complicate the scene, not dead-end the story. The fastest way to teach a table to think creatively is to consistently reward it; the fastest way to kill it is to meet good ideas with 'that's not what that skill does.' Especially with players new to tabletop, lean generous early — confidence to experiment is worth more than rules purity.

Raw physical power and gross-motor exertion — making your body overcome a problem through strength and stamina. Covers climbing, swimming, running and sprinting, sustained endurance movement (forced marches, long hauls), and pulling yourself or others up and over obstacles. It also owns raw force (the old Might): lifting and shifting heavy loads, forcing stuck doors, bent gates and jammed hatches, bracing or holding against pressure, breaking objects by sheer strength, restraining a struggling target by power, and the performance ceiling inside powered exosuits and heavy augmentation rigs. If the question is 'can your body's power or stamina overcome this?', it's Athletics. (Finesse and balance are Acrobatics; striking a person is Hand-to-Hand.)
examples: scaling a sheer hull to a hatch
swimming a flooded corridor against the current
prying a blast door open enough to slip through
bracing a collapsing beam while the team passes
carrying a wounded ally at a dead run
maxing a loader exosuit to lift a fallen girder
entries.sub: encumbrance and lift limits; exosuit and augmentation output ceiling; sustained exertion

entries.text: Finesse, agility, and total body control — movement problems solved by precision rather than power. Covers balance on narrow, slick, or unstable surfaces, tumbling and rolling, diving for cover, contortion through tight gaps, breaking falls and landing safely from height, tightrope and ledge work, vaulting cleanly, and evasive traversal through moving hazards or an active firefight. Where Athletics muscles through, Acrobatics threads the needle.
entries.sub: fall-damage mitigation, moving through difficult/contested terrain
examples: walking a girder across a chasm in a crosswind
tumbling under a closing blast door
contorting through a vent shaft
rolling with a two-story fall to halve the damage
vaulting a railing into cover mid-gunfight
keeping your feet as a ship pulls hard evasive maneuvers

entries.text: Unarmed close combat and the body as a weapon. Covers strikes (punches, kicks, knees, elbows, headbutts), grapples, throws, takedowns, holds, chokes, and hand disarms, plus natural and body-mounted weapons — claws, fangs, spurs, augmented body-blades. Includes choosing to subdue non-lethally and fighting in restrictive conditions (zero-g, tight corridors, while grappled). Armed melee is Melee Weapons.
examples: choking out a sentry silently from behind
pinning a panicking civilian without hurting them
trading blows in a bar brawl
grappling a knife-arm to control the blade
fighting in zero-g where footing is meaningless
using retractable claw augments as your main attack

entries.text: Armed close combat with anything in hand: blades, axes, clubs and blunt weapons, polearms and spears, energy and powered melee, shock batons, and improvised weapons (pipe, bottle, tool). Covers attacking, parrying and riposting, disarming, binding a weapon, and weapon-specific maneuvers and reach. Unarmed is Hand-to-Hand; thrown blades are Projectiles.
examples: dueling with a powered longsword
parrying a boarding pike and riposting
beating a guard down with a shock baton on stun
a console-side brawl with a length of pipe
using a polearm's reach to keep a bigger foe off you
disarming a knife-fighter with a blade bind

entries.text: Crew-served and heavy ordnance: machine guns and autocannons, rocket and missile launchers, mounted and vehicle turrets, artillery, man-portable heavy energy weapons, and the truly oversized. Covers setup and teardown, sustained and suppressing fire, heat and ammo management, and area/splash effects. It also owns destructive demolition — explosives or ordnance when the goal is simply to destroy, breach by force, or bring a structure down (the 'just make a hole' use). Surgical or render-safe explosive work is Engineering; personal firearms are Gunslinger/Marksman.
examples: laying suppressing fire to pin a squad
punching a missile through vehicle armor
setting a tripod autocannon to cover a hall
blowing a new doorway straight through a wall
managing barrel heat on a sustained burst
dropping a mortar on a fixed position

entries.text: Hands-on making, repairing, and modifying physical objects — mechanical work and the physical assembly of electronic gear. Covers field repair of weapons, armor, and vehicles, fashioning tools and parts from raw materials or scrap, building and assembling devices (including wiring up hardware someone designed), customizing and retrofitting, and patching pressure suits and hull breaches. The maker's hands: Engineering designs it, Fabrication builds and fixes it, Technology gets the electronics running.
entries.sub: repair (restore condition/function), crafting (time + materials + a design)
examples: clearing a jam and re-machining a worn firing pin in the field
welding a patch over a hull breach
building a custom weapon mount from scrap
fabricating a part no vendor stocks
reinforcing armor plating
jury-rigging a dead engine back to life

entries.text: Operating craft that fly: atmospheric flyers, shuttles, fighters, gunships, personal spacecraft, and the helm of small starships. Covers flight in atmosphere and vacuum, evasive maneuvers and dogfighting, docking, hard and emergency landings, and reentry. Plotting the actual course is Navigation; surface vehicles are Driving; a capital ship is a crew effort.
entries.sub: vehicle combat as pilot, stunt/maneuver checks
examples: threading a shuttle through a debris field
shaking a pursuing fighter with a hard break
docking manually after the autopilot dies
bringing a burning craft down in a survivable crash
flying nap-of-the-earth through a canyon to dodge sensors
a controlled reentry on a damaged heat shield

entries.text: Operating surface and ground vehicles: rovers, cars and trucks, hover-bikes and speeders, walkers and mechs, tracked vehicles, and watercraft. Covers handling at speed, ground chases, off-road and hazardous-terrain driving, ramming, evasive driving, and recovering from skids and rollovers. Flying craft are Piloting; planning the route is Navigation.
examples: outrunning a gang on hover-bikes through a packed market
ramming a roadblock at speed
walking a mech over unstable rubble
controlling a four-wheel slide on a wet ramp
running a skiff through rapids
using a truck as both cover and weapon in a running fight

entries.text: Finding and recovering value from the environment and the fallen. Covers identifying what's salvageable in wreckage and ruins, stripping useful components fast and under pressure, harvesting raw materials, looting gear and resources from defeated foes and abandoned sites, and spotting worth others walked past. Making new things is Fabrication; living off the land is Survival.
examples: stripping a downed gunship's still-charged cells before rivals arrive
spotting which corpse carries the keycard and the credits
pulling intact boards from a burned-out console
recognizing a 'worthless' crate as military salvage
field-stripping a wrecked rover for parts to fix yours

entries.text: Staying alive in any hostile environment — wild or built. Covers finding safe food, water, and shelter; reading weather and environmental hazards before they turn lethal; firecraft; tracking creatures and people; enduring hostile climates; and avoiding or handling dangerous wildlife. It equally covers urban survival: getting by in wastelands, ruins, sewers, dead zones, and on the street — scrounging shelter, reading the dangers of a derelict city, surviving rough. Survival keeps you alive in a place; Streetwise works that place's people.
examples: finding potable water on a parched moon
reading a coming dust storm in time to shelter
tracking a wounded beast to its den
surviving a week in a flooded sewer network
knowing which ruins flood at night and which collapse
treating exposure in the field

entries.text: The academic, theoretical knowledge of how civilized systems and people work: law and jurisprudence, economics and finance, politics and governance, and the behavioral sciences (psychology, sociology, anthropology). Covers knowing which laws apply and how serious a violation is, how bureaucracies, courts, and markets actually function, what an authority or institution would know or do, reading political and economic motives, and profiling behavior. Knowing a law exists and how bad breaking it is = Social Science; knowing who'll break it for you = Streetwise; current who's-who = Galactic Knowledge.
examples: spotting the loophole that voids a corp's claim
predicting how a market reacts to a leaked report
knowing which agency has jurisdiction and how to stall it
profiling a suspect from their background
arguing a felony down to a misdemeanor
reading the real power behind a puppet governor

entries.text: Investigation within and of digital and virtual environments — the digital detective. Covers tracing data trails, forensic reconstruction of logs and deleted files, profiling a target's digital behavior, following money through accounts, correlating metadata, and operating inside virtual/VR spaces, where Cyberintel can substitute for many non-physical checks. Breaking in is Hacking; the physical hardware is Technology.
entries.sub: the virtual-space substitution rule, digital forensics
examples: reconstructing who accessed a file from fragmented logs
following laundered credits through shell accounts
spotting a deepfake by its metadata
profiling an anonymous user from behavioral tells
investigating a crime scene inside a VR construct
proving a 'deleted' message still exists

entries.text: The design and conceptual side of building and breaking. Covers reading and producing structural and mechanical blueprints, calculating loads, stresses, and tolerances, identifying weak points, designing machines and systems, and reverse-engineering how something was made. It also owns controlled-outcome demolition: shaped charges, surgical breaching, dropping a structure precisely, and defusing or rendering ordnance safe — anywhere predicting the result matters. The hands-on build is Fabrication; raw 'just destroy it' explosives are Heavy Weapons; electronics are Technology.
entries.sub: design (a precondition for Fabrication), structural analysis, explosive calculation
examples: finding the one column whose loss drops a bridge and nothing else
designing the rig before the team builds it
sizing a charge to breach a vault without collapsing the room
defusing a pressure-triggered mine
spotting that a 'safe' catwalk won't hold the team
reverse-engineering a captured device

entries.text: Living, current knowledge of the galaxy as it is now — current events and worldly awareness at galactic scale. Covers who controls which sector, the active factions, corporations, and syndicates and their relationships, ongoing conflicts and recent events, prominent figures, and regional reputations: whether a planet has a bad rep, what it's known for, whether it's a war zone, and who nominally runs it. It tells you a station is mob-run and which cartel; it does not by itself find the specific fixer once you're there — that's Streetwise on arrival (or Social Science to reach the right official). Deep institutional theory is Social Science.
entries.sub: faction/figure recall, regional-reputation and recent-events recall
examples: knowing the two corps fighting over this sector and why
recognizing a faction insignia and what it implies
recalling a moon's black-market reputation
placing a notorious figure
knowing which border is a live shooting war
knowing a world's customs well enough not to arrive offensively

entries.text: Intrusion into protected digital systems — the active offense in cyberspace. Covers breaking encryption, defeating digital security, remote code execution, privilege escalation, planting and countering malware, hijacking networked devices and weapons mid-operation, spoofing credentials, and jamming signals. Investigating what's inside a system is Cyberintel; the physical electronics are Technology.
examples: cracking a maglock tied to the building network
seizing a hostile sentry turret in a firefight
spoofing a guard's credentials to open a door remotely
planting a timed logic bomb to wipe evidence
jamming an enemy squad's comms
brute-forcing an encrypted drive

entries.text: Keeping bodies alive and functioning, from battlefield first aid to full surgery. Covers stabilizing the dying, treating wounds and trauma, surgery and extraction, diagnosis, pharmacology and drug administration, countering poisons and managing toxic shock, sedation, and long-term care.
entries.sub: healing/stabilization, the consumables/drug subsystem, toxic-shock checks
examples: stopping a teammate bleeding out before the next round
extracting shrapnel and closing the wound
diagnosing an unknown illness from its symptoms
mixing the counter-agent for a poison
safely dosing combat stims without triggering toxic shock
field surgery by torchlight

entries.text: Finding your way and getting there — by any means and in any medium. Covers reading maps and charts; plotting and planning routes overland, by sea, through air, and across space (astrogation is one part of this skill, not the whole); orienteering and fixing position with or without instruments; estimating travel time and managing a journey's logistics; and routing around hazards so you arrive on time and intact. It is not only space travel — it's also not getting lost in trackless wilderness, a maze of streets, or a sprawling station. Operating the vehicle is Piloting/Driving; surviving the terrain is Survival.
entries.sub: route planning, ETA/logistics, position-fixing, jump/trajectory calculation
examples: plotting a fuel-efficient jump that avoids a patrolled lane
finding the fastest safe route across a hostile city
fixing position by the stars after instruments fail
timing a journey to arrive under cover of dark
reading a centuries-old tunnel map
picking the pass the storm won't close

entries.text: Scholarly knowledge of the supernatural — the study of magic rather than its use. Covers chi phenomena, spirit behavior, binding theory, spell mechanics, curses, and magical artifacts: an Occultist understands and can explain how magic works at a systemic level, whether or not they can cast a single spell themselves. Used to identify magical effects, research arcana, relics, and rituals, analyze bound spirits, recognize chi-based technology, and advise on or counter magical threats. The two who actually wield magic are the Spiritual caster (who commands it) and the Binder (who packages it into items).
examples: identifying what a glowing sigil will do before anyone touches it
recognizing a 'haunted' ship as a bound spirit and explaining how to free it
researching how to safely contain a cursed relic
advising the team on a chi-caster's likely capabilities
spotting chi-tech disguised as machinery
knowing — without necessarily performing — the ritual that breaks a ward

entries.text: The hard and natural sciences: chemistry, biology, botany, ecology, genetics, zoology, and physics. Covers analyzing unknown substances, developing antidotes, compounds, and reagents, identifying organisms and pathogens, studying ecosystems and toxins, explaining natural phenomena, and designing experiments. The soft/social sciences are Social Science; treating patients is Medicine; built machines and structures are Engineering.
examples: identifying an unknown powder and what it does
synthesizing an antidote from local flora
judging whether an alien organism is hostile or edible
analyzing why a reactor's coolant is degrading
sequencing a pathogen to design a countermeasure
predicting a reaction before mixing two volatile agents

entries.text: Working with electronic and computing hardware. Covers installing, configuring, modifying, repairing, and operating electronic devices and systems; security hardware and electronic countermeasures; sensors and scanners; the physical side of networked infrastructure; and safely installing and activating cybernetics. This is the electronics expertise — building or crafting a device from scratch is Fabrication, software intrusion is Hacking, digital investigation is Cyberintel.
entries.sub: device repair/modification, electronic (hardware) security, cybernetics activation
examples: defeating an electronic lock at the panel instead of over the network
installing a cyber-arm without rejection or shock
tuning a sensor suite to catch a cloaked signature
setting up jammers and countermeasures around a camp
modifying a scanner to detect a specific material
safely powering up salvaged tech that might be trapped

entries.text: Presenting a crafted version of yourself to an audience — being someone or something you're not, convincingly. Covers acting and sustained impersonation, assuming and holding a false identity under scrutiny, disguise (altering appearance to look like someone or something else), projecting or faking emotion, and the performing arts: singing, dancing, instruments, oratory, showmanship. Staying unseen entirely is Stealth; lying in the moment in conversation is Subterfuge.
examples: passing as a uniformed officer at a checkpoint
holding a cover identity through a long dinner with people who knew the real person
disguising as maintenance to walk past security
weeping on cue to sell a story
playing a set well enough to be welcomed backstage
impersonating a noble's voice and manner

entries.text: Positive interpersonal influence — getting people to like and trust you. Covers building rapport and strong first impressions, warmth and likeability, flirtation to gain access, putting anxious or angry people at ease, smoothing over friction and insults, and cultivating personal contacts and goodwill. One-on-one or small groups. Coercion by fear is Intimidation; bargaining is Negotiation; swaying crowds is Leadership.
examples: talking a wary guard into a friendly chat
making a great impression on a potential patron
calming a panicking witness enough to help
flirting past a velvet rope
defusing a bar argument before it turns to blows
turning a one-time contact into a reliable friend

entries.text: Coercion through fear and force of presence — compliance because the alternative frightens. Covers explicit and implicit threats, menace, interrogation by pressure, ultimatums, extortion, staring someone down, and demoralizing enemies in combat (morale damage). The friendly counterpart is Charm; bargaining is Negotiation.
examples: making a witness talk by implying the cost of silence
staring down a thug until he backs off
shaking down a vendor for protection
breaking a prisoner's resolve in interrogation
barking orders that scatter a panicked crowd
demoralizing an enemy line until it breaks

entries.text: The transactional, deal-making social skill. Covers haggling over price, brokering deals and contracts, structuring terms and partnerships, trade and pricing, mediation between parties, and securing surrenders or hostage releases. Where Charm makes people like you and Intimidation makes them afraid, Negotiation makes a deal both sides will keep.
examples: haggling a fence down to a fair cut
structuring a contract the corp can't wriggle out of
mediating a truce between two gangs
talking a cornered enemy into surrender on terms
arranging passage in exchange for a favor
brokering a salvage sale without getting fleeced

entries.text: Knowledge and correct execution of formal customs across cultures and species. Covers etiquette, ceremony, diplomatic ritual, court and corporate hierarchy, religious observance, and the thousand ways an outsider can give (or avoid) offense in formal and multicultural settings — moving through formal spaces without triggering the wrong response. Raw likeability is Charm; current who's-who is Galactic Knowledge.
examples: greeting an alien dignitary correctly
knowing which gesture is a grave insult to a Skalander elder
navigating a gala's seating and precedence
presenting credentials properly to win an audience
observing a religious rite without blasphemy
dressing and behaving correctly at a noble court

entries.text: Interacting with and commanding magic directly — the innate caster's path. Spirits and paranormal phenomena are raw emotion given form; the Spiritualist taps their own CHI or the CHI of the environment and the spirits within it, merging with that force and bending it to their will. For casters: casting chi spells, channeling and managing chi pools, and sustaining active effects. For non-casters: sensing chi in living beings and places, detecting active magical effects, reading the spiritual and emotional states of beings with strong chi, and resisting chi-based compulsion. This is the path that becomes one with magic and commands it — the Binder instead exploits magic as a resource, and the Occultist only studies it.
entries.sub: the chi/magic subsystem, the chi pool
examples: channeling chi to mend a wound or strike at range
calming a raw-emotion spirit by meeting it with your own chi
sensing the chi signature of someone hiding nearby
detecting that a room is under an active spell
reading whether calm is genuine or chi-masked
meditating to recover spent chi

entries.text: Working the urban underworld and street ecosystem. Covers finding the fixers, fences, dealers, and off-books services willing to help; knowing who to talk to and who to avoid; gathering rumors and black-market intel; reading gang and criminal territory; spotting a setup before it springs; and blending into and moving through cities and undercities. Knowing someone will do the deal = Streetwise; knowing how illegal and serious it is = Social Science; surviving the physical place = Survival.
examples: finding a back-alley surgeon who won't report a gunshot
knowing which blocks belong to which crew
catching the rumor that a shipment is about to move
sensing a 'too good' deal is a trap
locating a fence for hot goods
passing through a slum without being marked an outsider

entries.text: Active deception — the telling of convincing falsehoods. Covers lying convincingly, bluffing, conning, spinning cover stories, misdirection, deflecting accusations, and working a mark. This is purely the offense of deceit; catching someone else's lie and reading their intent is Insight, and sustained identity or disguise is Performance.
examples: bluffing past a checkpoint with a confident lie
running a long con on a greedy mark
spinning a cover story on the spot when challenged
misdirecting a guard with a fabricated emergency
deflecting a pointed accusation without flinching
planting a believable false lead for an investigator

entries.text: Moving groups of people — command and mass influence. Covers commanding and rallying allies and followers, giving orders under fire, restoring and bolstering morale (including the in-combat morale heal), and inspiring coordinated action; and at scale, swaying crowds, building or wrecking reputations, and running propaganda and influence campaigns. One-on-one warmth is Charm.
entries.sub: morale support, the Clout/Reputation track (per-faction standing this skill moves), crowd effects
examples: rallying a wavering squad to hold the line
steadying a panicking group so they act instead of freeze
giving crisp orders that coordinate a complex assault
swaying a crowd to your side at a rally
running a rumor campaign to turn a district against a rival
building a reputation that opens doors before you arrive

entries.text: Reading people — the defensive mirror of Subterfuge. Covers discerning emotional state, sincerity, motive, and intent; sensing when someone is lying to or conning you; gauging reactions and disposition; and sensing when someone is dangerous or about to act. Where Subterfuge tells the lie, Insight catches it; where Awareness reads the physical room, Insight reads the people in it.
entries.sub: opposed against the deceiver's Subterfuge; the GM-read hook (once per rank, ask the GM a straight read on a person or whether a scene is a trap)
examples: catching the micro-tell that a contact is lying
reading that a calm negotiator is about to walk
sensing which stranger in the room is the real threat
gauging whether an NPC can be trusted with the plan
noticing someone is being coerced behind their words
feeling that a friendly offer is bait

entries.text: Passive, defensive perception — not getting caught out. Covers noticing without actively searching: sensing an ambush before it springs, catching that you're being watched, tailed, or scouted, registering that something in a space has changed or is 'off,' and spotting a hidden watcher in passing. It is the counter to someone else's Stealth and to Tactics-style scouting. Deliberately searching for hidden things is Search; reading people is Insight; doing the scouting yourself is Tactics.
examples: feeling the wrong kind of quiet before stepping into a trap
catching the glint of a sniper's scope
noticing the guard rotation is off tonight
sensing you've picked up a tail in the market
registering that a crate wasn't there an hour ago
waking at the faint sound that shouldn't be there

entries.text: Active, deliberate looking — what you find when you decide to look. Covers methodically searching a room, person, or object for what's hidden: concealed doors and compartments, planted items, contraband, and clues; and forensic, careful examination. The passive 'something's wrong' sense is Awareness.
examples: finding the wall safe behind the painting
tossing a suspect's quarters for a data chip
locating the pressure plate before stepping on it
recovering a clue others walked past
finding the seam of a concealed hatch
discovering what's sewn into a coat's lining

entries.text: Avoiding detection entirely. Covers moving silently, hiding yourself and objects, camouflage, masking signatures (heat, EM, sound), activating and using cloaking tech, breaking line of sight, and setting up ambushes or staying unseen while tailing a mark. Looking like you belong (disguise) is Performance; this is about not being seen at all.
examples: crossing a guarded yard without tripping a sensor or an eye
hiding a body before the patrol returns
tailing a target through a crowd unseen
masking your heat from a drone's thermal sweep
setting an ambush and holding dead still
slipping a weapon past a pat-down

entries.text: Precise hands and physical security — the thief's and infiltrator's manual craft. Covers sleight of hand, pickpocketing, palming and planting objects, and defeating physical security: picking locks, cracking safes, mechanical bypass, and disabling manual traps and alarms, plus fine-motor work under pressure. Digital locks and network security are Hacking/Technology; thrown weapons are Projectiles.
examples: picking a mechanical lock in the dark before the patrol turns
lifting a keycard from a mark's pocket
planting a tracking bug unnoticed
cracking an old wall safe by feel
disarming a tripwire by hand
palming the real chip and leaving a fake

entries.text: Precision thrown and muscle-powered ranged weapons. Covers throwing knives, grenades, and thrown gadgets, plus bows, crossbows, and slings — everything about accuracy, arc, lead, and timing for ranged weapons that aren't firearms. Firearms are Gunslinger (sidearms) and Marksman (long guns); heavy ordnance is Heavy Weapons.
examples: landing a grenade through a moving vehicle's window
pinning a guard with a thrown knife
arcing a frag over cover onto a clustered squad
a silent crossbow bolt to drop a sentry
bouncing a thrown charge around a corner
leading a running target with a bow

entries.text: Personal short-arms: pistols, SMGs, and shotguns. Covers quick-draw, close-quarters gunplay, snap and reflex shots, hip-fire, dual-wielding sidearms, and clearing jams fast. Long-range rifle work is Marksman; thrown weapons are Projectiles.
examples: out-drawing an opponent in a standoff
clearing a room with a shotgun
snap-firing at a target that breaks cover
dual-wielding pistols in a close melee
hip-firing an SMG while moving
clearing a jam and getting back in the fight without missing a beat

entries.text: Long-range firearms: rifles and sniper systems. Covers precision fire, range and wind estimation, sustained accuracy at distance, called shots to specific parts or equipment, building and holding a shooting position, and breath control. Sidearms are Gunslinger; thrown weapons are Projectiles.
examples: a one-shot kill on a sentry from a rooftop nest
estimating wind and drop across a valley
placing a round through a target's weapon to disarm without killing
holding a sight picture while waiting for the signal
covering the team's advance from overwatch
timing a breath-held shot between heartbeats

entries.text: Remote operation of devices as an extension of yourself: drones, robots, remote turrets, manipulator arms, and nanotech swarms. While operating, the device performs as though you were aboard it — for reconnaissance, combat, or task work. Hacking into someone else's device is Hacking; your own body's installed tech is Technology.
examples: flying a recon drone ahead to map a compound
piloting a combat drone into a fight you stay clear of
using a remote arm to defuse a hazard from a safe distance
running a swarm of micro-drones to search a building
taking over a fixed turret you control
sending a bot through a gap too small for a person

entries.text: Understanding and winning engagements, before and during — the active, offensive side of the engagement game. Before contact: scouting and surveilling a target, mapping patrols and security layouts, observing routines, setting up an ambush, and turning it into an approach plan. In contact: reading the flow of a fight, identifying enemy weaknesses, positioning, setting kill zones, prioritizing targets, and exploiting openings. Noticing that you're the one being scouted or ambushed is the defensive mirror, Awareness.
entries.sub: the scout-plan-exploit chain, ambush setup, tactical bonuses
examples: watching a compound for a day and mapping the guard rotation
choosing the approach that avoids the strongest defenses
setting an ambush where numbers don't help the enemy
calling the shot that collapses their formation
spotting which foe to drop first to break their plan
adapting on the fly when contact goes loud

entries.text: Artificer magic — magic treated as a refined, exploitable resource rather than an innate gift. Where the Spiritualist merges with and commands magic, the Binder packages it: capturing and binding spirits and chi into objects to make spell shards, charged relics, and bound-spirit devices — in effect, disposable magic that even a mundane person with no power of their own can pick up and use. Covers the know-how to design and craft such items, charge and use them, bind spirits into objects or places, and reverse or disrupt existing bindings and wards. For non-casters: detecting bound spirits and arcane signatures, identifying cursed or bound objects, and resisting possession and arcane compulsion. Knowledge of how it all works is Occultism; the innate-caster path is Spiritual.
entries.sub: the arcane/binding subsystem, spirit-binding contests, item creation and charges
examples: crafting single-use spell shards the whole squad can throw
binding a troublesome spirit into a containment vessel
charging a ward-stone anyone can plant
handing a mundane ally a relic that lets them cast once
disrupting an enemy's bound device
identifying a cursed item before someone triggers it

entries.text: SKILL BOUNDARIES (GM quick rulings)
Goal is to destroy / breach / level it: HEAVY WEAPONS. Goal is a controlled, predicted outcome (shaped charge, surgical breach, defuse): ENGINEERING.
Building or crafting any device: FABRICATION. Configuring, securing, repairing, or operating electronics: TECHNOLOGY. Designing it: ENGINEERING.

Academic / legal knowledge (which law, how serious): SOCIAL SCIENCE. A place or faction's reputation and current events: GALACTIC KNOWLEDGE. Who is willing to do it and who to avoid, on the ground: STREETWISE.
Telling the lie: SUBTERFUGE. Catching the lie and reading the person: INSIGHT.
Noticing you are being scouted or ambushed (defense): AWARENESS. Doing the scouting or setting the ambush (offense): TACTICS. Deliberately searching for hidden things: SEARCH.
Not being seen at all: STEALTH. Being seen but as someone else (disguise, acting): PERFORMANCE. Talking your way through: SUBTERFUGE.

When a scene tips into a challenge - a firefight, a chase, a frantic race against a closing door - you resolve it in ROUNDS. Before the first round, two things happen in order: you check for SURPRISE, then you roll INITIATIVE.

Decide whether either side is caught unaware. If one side springs an ambush or is simply oblivious, the aware side has surprise. The surprised side is limited to a single STANDARD or MOVE action (no complex actions, no reactions) for the first round only; from the second round on, everyone acts normally. If nobody is surprised, go straight to initiative.

Initiative is the one roll in the entire game that is NOT success-based. Instead of counting 5s, you roll a number of D10 equal to your WITS and add up the pips on the dice. Highest total acts first, then down the line. So WITS 3 means 3D10 totalled - a range of 3 to 30.
examples: WITS 3 -> roll 3D10 and total them (3-30). WITS 5 -> 5D10 (5-50).
Ties: tied characters act at the same time. If it genuinely matters who goes first, the tied parties roll a fresh initiative just to settle that single moment, re-rolling until the tie breaks.
entries.sub: GM: this flat-total initiative is a deliberately provisional system - swingy by design and still being tuned. For a big mob, feel free to roll once for the whole group or assign a fixed order to keep things moving.

entries.key: THE MAINTENANCE PHASE (start of every round)
entries.text: Each round opens with maintenance, resolved by everyone before turns begin: attempt a RECOVER against each AILMENT affecting you, and pay the upkeep on - or end - any effect you are sustaining.
After maintenance, combatants take their turns in initiative order (highest WITS total first). On your turn you draw from the following action types, in whatever sensible order the moment calls for:
Fast, reflexive things. They can be taken at almost any point on your turn, but never before the maintenance phase has resolved.
Your move for the round. You may delay it - if you do, it resolves at the very end of the round (see Delayed Movement below).
Your bread-and-butter action: most attacks, a skill use, working a device. Most turns are built around one standard action.

A COMPLEX action is not a separate slot - it is your STANDARD action turned all the way up. To take one, sacrifice either your QUICK action or your MOVE action; that sacrifice is what upgrades your standard action into a complex action.
Extra actions granted by SURGES, talents, or powers, when applicable - spent on top of your normal turn.
If you held your move, or you are RUNNING, take that movement now, after everyone has acted.
Initiative also settles split-second clashes: when one action would interrupt or react to another, the higher initiative total resolves first. This is the only time mid-round order is contested.

Make surprise worth chasing - reward players who scout, ambush, or talk their way into the first move, and let a blown approach hand surprise to the other side. Treat the initiative total as a quick gate, not a sacred number: it is intentionally rough, so don't let the math stall the table, and house-rule ties however keeps the fight flowing.

entries.key: DICE SUCCESS - THE CORE OF EVERY ROLL
entries.text: Almost everything resolves the same way: you build a pool of D10s, roll it, and count SUCCESSES. Unless a rule says otherwise, every die showing 5 or higher (5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10) is one success; 1 through 4 are failures. You succeed when your successes meet or beat the task's DC.

Counting 5s rather than adding numbers keeps results readable at a glance and makes a bigger, more skilled pool reliably better without runaway math. The single exception is INITIATIVE, which totals the dice - every other roll in the game counts successes.
examples: Skill 4 vs DC 2: roll 4D10, you need any 2 dice to land on 5+.

entries.text: When you call for a roll, say the pool and the DC out loud ('roll your Larceny, DC 5') so the player knows the stakes before the dice hit the table. If a task has no real chance of meaningful failure, don't call for a roll at all.

entries.key: SKILL DC - HOW HARD CAN IT BE?
entries.text: A task's DC is the number of successes it takes to pull off. The harder the thing, the more 5s you need. DCs run from 1 (trivial) to 10 (the ceiling) - and 10 is a hard cap: nothing is ever rated higher, and no roll can ever need more than 10 successes.

At the table you rarely need the full ladder. Most checks fall into three bands: DC 3 trivial, DC 5 standard, DC 7 hard. Reach for those first and only fine-tune when a task is clearly easier or nastier than usual.

entries.key: WHEN IN DOUBT, OFFER MORE THAN ONE ROAD
entries.text: A locked door, a hostile crowd, a sealed vault - most obstacles can be cracked by several skills at a fair DC. Set the number by what the player wants to achieve, not by the obstacle alone, and let any plausible approach roll. (See the Skills section.)

rows: Anyone can do this without thinking.
Basic stuff - a novice manages it.
Trivial for a trained hand (the practical "easy").
Challenging - the standard call for a real test.
Really difficult; few people manage it.
Nobel-prize stuff; the best in the field.
Impossible. The cap is always 10; no roll can need more than 10 successes.

entries.text: When an attack connects - its hit successes cleared your DEFENSE - you work out how much actually gets through. Defence comes in two stages: first the attack has to HIT, then it has to beat your one defensive layer. What gets past is shaped by the attack's two numbers (DAMAGE and POWER), its DAMAGE TYPE, your defensive layer, and your own ENDURANCE or WILLPOWER.

entries.key: DAMAGE TYPE - IT DECIDES EVERYTHING ELSE
entries.text: Every attack has a damage type: PHYSICAL, ENERGY, TECH, or SPIRITUAL. The type does two jobs. First, it picks which of your defence's four ratings applies - the same layer can be tough against bullets (Physical) and feeble against a hacker's feedback (Tech). Second, it decides whether the attack wounds your HEALTH or your MORALE - which in turn sets whether you soak with ENDURANCE (health) or WILLPOWER (morale).
The raw damage dealt once a hit clears defenses - the size of the wound before the defence rating and SOAK get their say.

The attack's penetrating force, measured against your defence's rating for that damage type. Each point POWER sits ABOVE the rating cancels a point of SOAK - that damage gets through automatically; each point BELOW reduces the incoming damage by one.

You carry exactly ONE layer of defence: armour, a forcefield, a datacom, or a (spiritual) barrier. Whatever it is, it gives you a DEFENSE RATING - Low, Medium, High or Extreme - rated separately against Physical, Energy, Tech and Spiritual damage, plus a SOAK pool. You no longer stack a forcefield on top of armour; you pick your one layer and live with its strengths and gaps.

Your layer's SOAK is a dice pool (written like 4D + 0) you roll to shrug off damage - rolled together with ENDURANCE against HEALTH attacks, or with WILLPOWER against MORALE attacks. Each success removes one point of incoming damage; reduce the damage to 0 and the hit is fully absorbed, with no further effects checked.
Work the hit through in order:
1) Note the attack's DAMAGE TYPE and whether it targets HEALTH or MORALE, then roll the weapon's DAMAGE.
2) Compare POWER to your defence rating for that damage type. Each point of POWER above the rating cancels a point of SOAK (automatic damage); each point below reduces the damage.
3) Roll SOAK + ENDURANCE (for HEALTH attacks) or SOAK + WILLPOWER (for MORALE attacks) and remove that many points from the remaining damage.
4) Whatever damage is left comes off the targeted pool - HEALTH or MORALE.

Hitting is not all-or-nothing. Count the hit-successes you score BEYOND your target's DEFENSE - the number you actually needed to land the blow. Each surplus success adds +1 damage, capped by your weapon's EXPERTISE rating, and this payoff applies chiefly on COMPLEX actions. Expertise is the system's standing reward for skill: roll well past what you needed and you unlock more of the weapon; scrape a bare hit and you get none of it.
examples: Needed 3 successes to hit, scored 6. The 3 surplus successes add +3 damage - but only up to the weapon's EXPERTISE; a weapon with EXPERTISE 2 caps that bonus at +2.

entries.key: TRAUMA - WHEN ONE HIT OVERWHELMS YOU
entries.text: If a single hit's final damage exceeds the target's ENDURANCE (for HEALTH damage) or WILLPOWER (for MORALE damage), it inflicts a TRAUMA - a lasting wound that escalates GRAVE -> MORTAL -> DYING. The trigger is one big hit beating your attribute in a single blow, not your pool grinding down to zero.
examples: ENDURANCE 4, a hit deals 6 HEALTH damage after mitigation -> 6 > 4, so it inflicts a trauma.

entries.key: CRITICAL AILMENTS COME FROM CRITICAL HITS, NOT TRAUMA
entries.text: A common mix-up worth nailing down: Critical Ailments (Bleed, Exposed, Knockdown, Sick, Dazed) are NOT caused by trauma. They are inflicted only by a CRITICAL HIT - a natural 10 on the luck die. Trauma wounds you; the crit is what stamps an ailment on top. (See Critical Ailments.)

Damage type is your richest dial: lead enemies with the type a party is weak against, and reward players who switch weapons or layers to cover a gap. Because everyone now runs a single defensive layer, telegraph what a foe is wearing (or projecting) so the choice of how to punch through it is an interesting one, not a guess.

Thrown and arced attacks - grenades, satchel charges, anything you lob - never simply vanish on a miss. They land somewhere. If your roll falls short of the DC, the LUCK die (your first die) tells you which way the throw drifts, and it scatters 1 metre (one square) for every point you missed the DC by.
examples: Thrown at DC 5, you score 2 successes -> missed by 3 -> it lands 3 metres away, in the luck-die direction.

entries.text: Picture the target dead ahead of you, at the centre of a clock face. Your luck die points the drift:

Deviation keeps thrown weapons thrilling and a little dangerous - a botched grenade (a 6-7) can roll back toward the thrower's own feet. Measure the drift, drop the blast where it actually lands, and resolve whatever it catches.

rows: Long - overshoots straight past the target.

entries.key: ENEMY TYPES - HOW TOUGH IS IT?
entries.text: Not every foe is built like a player character. To keep fights fast, most NPCs are graded by how much punishment it takes to drop them. The four tiers below tell you, at a glance, how lethal a given enemy is and how much spotlight it deserves.

These tiers gauge relative toughness, nothing more - an enemy can break tier when it makes sense (a brilliant street doc with a high Medicine skill but no fight in them). Anchor the numbers with the compendium's Enemy Generator, then bend them to fit the character.

Mix tiers to control a fight's rhythm: a wall of Henchmen makes players feel powerful, a single Elite or Boss makes them sweat. Henchmen are meant to fall fast - don't slow the table rolling their soak when one clean hit should end them.

rows: Cannon fodder; meant to fall fast and in numbers.
Also gets QUICK actions - faster and deadlier.
Full talents, EVO, actions and surges. Run them as a PC.

entries.text: A typical character comfortably carries about 10 units of gear - roughly 50 kg - and your PHYSIQUE shifts that by 5 kg per point (so each unit is about 5 kg). Above your carry you can still heave things for a moment: you can LIFT up to 5 times your carry off the ground, and PUSH or DRAG up to 10 times your carry along it.
examples: Physique +2 -> 50 + 10 = 60 kg carry; lift ~300 kg, push or drag ~600 kg.

entries.text: Every item also has a SIZE, which tells you how much room it eats, how easily it hides, and whether you can carry it by hand at all. Sizes climb a fixed ladder; the bigger the item, the more of your capacity it swallows and the harder it is to conceal or move.

Lead with the fiction: a Colossal weapon simply does not fit through a maintenance hatch, and a Huge crate needs a cart or a second pair of hands no matter what the math says. Use size as a soft pressure on what the party can haul out, not a spreadsheet to audit every pocket.

rows: Palmed and pocketed - a chip, a vial, a holdout blade.
One-handed and easily stowed - a pistol, a datapad.
Two hands or a backpack - a rifle, a toolkit.
Bulky, often two-handed - a heavy weapon, a sealed case.
Awkward to carry alone; wants a strap, a rig, or help.
Needs a cart, a mount, or several people to move.
Vehicle-scale; not carried by hand at all.
Structure- or ship-scale; moved only by machinery.

entries.key: AVAILABILITY - HOW HARD IS IT TO FIND?
entries.text: Availability is about scarcity: how hard a thing is to track down at all. To get hold of something, players search for vendors, lean on contacts, or just ask around the right circles - the GM sets a DC by how rare the item is.
On any shelf. No real effort to find.
A little looking - the right shop or a quick ask around.
Specialist vendors and the right contacts only.
Tight supply: waitlists, permits, or the right connections.
One of a kind. You don't buy it - you find it, win it, or take it.

entries.key: LEGALITY - HOW MUCH TROUBLE IS IT TO HOLD?
entries.text: Separate from how rare a thing is, is whether you are allowed to have it. Legality decides who comes knocking when you are caught with it - and a Common item can still be wildly Illegal. Read both numbers before you flash something around.

Availability and legality stack into texture: a Common-but-Illegal weapon floods the gutters but gets you arrested; a Rare-but-Legal tool is simply hard to source. Let contacts, black markets, and permits be the playground where the two interact.

table.title: Legality
rows: Owned and carried freely, no questions asked. (Item cards label these "No Permit".)
Legal only with the right permit or licence; carrying it without one invites fines or confiscation.
Outlawed for civilians - possession alone is a crime.
Beyond illegal: military, corporate, or state-secret hardware. Being caught with it draws the worst kind of attention.

entries.text: On every skill check and every defense, single out one die as your LUCK die - by convention, the first one you rolled. It works no matter how the rest of the pool lands: a natural 1 is a CRIT FAILURE, and a natural 10 is a CRIT SUCCESS.

A roll here is rarely a flat pass or fail - how far you clear the DC, or fall short of it, usually matters. Beat the DC handily and you tend to do more (extra successes can mean extra effect, like more damage); scrape a miss and it costs you far less than a total whiff. The luck die marks the two outer extremes of that scale - a natural 1 or a natural 10 - while everything between them is the realm of GRADED success and failure. The clearest worked version of this idea sits just below in Graded Saves, where the size of your shortfall sets the severity band.

A crit success can lift a near-miss into a clean win or stamp a Critical Ailment onto a foe; a crit failure complicates even an otherwise successful roll. Luck reaches past combat, too - it steers a missed throw's DEVIATION and the swing on a failed SAVE.

Crits are your licence to make a moment memorable. On a crit success, give the player a little extra; on a crit failure, introduce a complication rather than just 'nothing happens' - a jam, a noise, an opening for the enemy.

entries.key: SURGE - YOUR EDGE WHEN IT COUNTS
entries.text: Surge is a small pool of momentum you spend to bend a moment your way. You begin every game with 1 surge point.

Beyond your starting point, surge is a reward: the GM hands it out for outstanding roleplay or for simply doing something awesome at the table - think of it as the game paying you back for the moments that make a session. Your cap is the higher of your ENDURANCE or WILLPOWER; any surge earned past that cap is lost.
You cannot pour your whole pool into one scene: you may spend at most your choice of SPEED or WITS surges per SCENE.
Spend a surge for exactly ONE of the following:
examples: An additional STANDARD, MOVE, or QUICK action on your current turn (one extra action only).
Roll a skill twice and keep whichever of the two results you prefer.
Nudge your luck die to remove a CRITICAL FAILURE.
entries.sub: Some talents change how your surges work - watch for them when building a character.

entries.text: Surge is your reward currency, so spend it freely: hand a point to the player who leaned hard into their character or pulled off something memorable, and the whole table will start chasing those moments. It is a feedback loop that pays players for exactly the play you want to see.
GRADED SAVES

A SAVE is a defensive check against an effect (toxin, suffocation, shock, fear, mental compulsion, etc.). Roll your save pool — ENDURANCE for HEALTH/body effects, WILLPOWER for MORALE/mind effects (an effect may name another pool) — and count successes against the effect's SAVE DC. No skill is rolled for a save. What matters is not pass/fail but BY HOW MUCH you miss, the same way a weapon's POWER cuts through SOAK.
Successes equal to or above the DC: the effect is AVOIDED entirely.
On a miss, the SHORTFALL (DC minus your successes) sets the severity band. An effect only needs to define these bands once, instead of a separate result for every possible margin.
Shortfall 1 (SMALL band): a brush. Shortest duration, lowest tier, or a SMALL penalty only.
Shortfall 2 (MEDIUM band): a reduced version of the effect, or a MEDIUM penalty.
Shortfall 3 (HIGH band): the effect applies as written.
Shortfall 4 or more (EXTREME band): the effect applies in full plus its escalation or critical rider.

Consistent with the luck quadrants: a CRIT FAILURE (luck die 1) on a FAILED save is always OVERWHELMED regardless of shortfall. A CRIT SUCCESS (luck die 10) on a FAILED save still lands but one band lighter AND grants a small advantage (act first next round, or learn the source). On a SUCCESSFUL save, a CRIT FAILURE still avoids the effect but leaves a faint SMALL trace briefly (mitigated success), and a CRIT SUCCESS also cleanses one existing same-track ailment.

Because severity scales with shortfall, a small save pool is no longer a binary pass/fail cliff: a near miss costs little, and every point of ENDURANCE/WILLPOWER softens every ailment by lowering your shortfall. If the SAVE DC exceeds your pool you can still only fail, but a higher attribute keeps the band low.

A Critical Ailment is a nasty status rider inflicted by a CRITICAL HIT (a natural 10 on the luck die) - not by trauma. Which ailment lands depends on the damage type that scored the crit, so the same crit feels different from a flamethrower, a railgun, or a psychic lash.

Because ailments ride on crits, they should feel like punctuation - sudden and vivid. Call them out by name and describe them ('the round punches through and she's BLEEDING'), and remember most stack or escalate if re-applied, so a drawn-out fight gets nastier on its own.

rows: Gain damage vulnerability 1 to all (cumulative if re-applied).
1 damage per maintenance phase (cumulative if re-applied).
Knocked down, cancels COMPLEX actions; the target counts as PRONE.
SMALL penalty to all rolls (not cumulative if re-applied).
Cannot perform quick actions (becomes STUNNED if re-applied while dazed).

entries.text: Worlds spin at wildly different rates, so trade and travel run on a single base-10 standard rather than any one planet's clock. Everything counts in tens, which makes the calendar easy to do in your head.
A day is 10 hours. A week is 10 days. A month is 10 weeks, or 100 days. A year is 10 months - 100 weeks, or 1,000 days.
Days and months carry no official names; most people just use the numbers. A date reads day-month-year, so 'day 8, month 8, year 5734' is written 08-08-5734.

entries.key: A WORKING LIFE - FOR THE LUCKY FEW
entries.text: On paper, standard full-time work runs 10 hours on, then 10 hours off - one day working, one day resting, about 50 hours a week, half your waking time on the clock. That tidy arrangement is for the lucky few, which is to say the very few. Most corporations squeeze their people until they drop: sleep replicators, stim-cocktails, and wakefulness drugs to keep a body productive almost around the clock are common tools, not scandals, and a worker's contract rarely protects them from any of it. In the 56th Century, real rest is a perk you earn or buy - not a right you are owed.

Lean on the tens when you narrate downtime and travel - 'three days out, a hundred hours of jump' lands cleanly and reinforces that this is not Earth. Tie deadlines and shifts to the calendar to make the setting feel lived-in.

Every item in the compendium - a pistol, a vest, a vial, a starship - is presented as a stat card. Most of the card is shared vocabulary you only need to learn once; the rest is specific to what the thing does. This section walks the stat lines for each kind of gear so you can read any card at a glance.

Four lines show up on almost everything. COST is the price in credits. SIZE is how much room it takes and how easily it hides. AVAILABILITY is how hard it is to find, and LEGALITY is how much trouble it is to own. Size, availability and legality are all covered under the Basic Rules (Carrying Capacity & Item Size, and Availability) - learn them once and they read the same on a knife or a frigate.

entries.key: EXPERTISE - A SHARED STAT, AND A DESIGN PHILOSOPHY
entries.text: One line recurs across most usable gear: EXPERTISE, the measure of how much skill an item rewards. It is no longer a melee-only trait - weapons, datacoms and other active gear all carry it. Mechanically, successes you roll beyond a task's DC convert into a better result (on a weapon, bonus damage up to the item's expertise), so the better you roll, the more of the item you unlock.

entries.key: WHY SOME ITEMS HAVE LOW STATS AND HIGH EXPERTISE
entries.text: Expertise is also a deliberate design lever, so read it as a clue to who an item is for. Some gear is built with intentionally modest base stats but high expertise: these are specialists' tools, clumsy and underwhelming in untrained hands and exceptional in trained ones. A novice barely clears the DC and unlocks none of the ceiling, while an expert rolls successes to spare and turns them into real power. When you see a low-stat, high-expertise item, read it as 'only worth carrying if you are good with it' - and when you build a character, let your best skills point you toward the gear that rewards them.

entries.key: SPECIAL PROPERTIES LIVE IN THE GLOSSARY
entries.text: Many items carry a SPECIAL line - short tags like DP, AEGIS, DISCRETE, EMP, HARDENED. These are named properties shared across the catalogue, not rules unique to one item, and every one has a full definition in the Glossary. When a card shows a tag you don't recognise, look it up there rather than expecting it spelled out on the card.
A weapon's card tells you how hard it hits, what kind of hit it is, how far, how fast, and how reliably. Here is every line.
How much damage the weapon deals once a hit clears defenses - the size of the wound before SOAK. (See Damage & Defense.)
The attack's penetrating force, measured against the target's defence rating for this weapon's damage type: each point above the rating cancels a point of SOAK, each point below softens the hit.
Physical, Energy, Tech or Spiritual. It decides which of a defence's four ratings applies and whether the hit lands on HEALTH (soak with ENDURANCE) or MORALE (soak with WILLPOWER).

Three range bands. Most weapons are at their best in one band and take penalties reaching past it, and for melee weapons 'range' is your reach. Some weapons - shotguns above all - instead adjust their POWER by range bracket, hitting hardest up close and weakening with distance.
Whether the weapon can fire single shots, BURST, or FULL AUTO. What each does depends on the action you spend to fire - burst and full auto trade extra ammo for extra dice or extra targets.
How many shots sit in the magazine - or the charge an energy weapon's power cell holds - before you must reload or let it cool.
The action you must spend to reload, or the time an energy weapon needs to recharge its ammo (usually rounds, sometimes whole scenes).

How much skill the weapon rewards. Hit-successes beyond the DC convert into bonus damage, up to this rating, chiefly on COMPLEX actions. A low-damage, high-expertise weapon is a specialist's piece - poor in untrained hands, lethal in skilled ones (see Reading Your Gear).

Whether the weapon is wielded in one hand or needs both. This tells you what your off-hand is free to do - hold a shield, a second weapon, a datapad - and how easily the weapon is carried or hidden. It is not a damage modifier.

Melee weapons work just like firearms, with a single swap: REACH stands in for range.
